beats.intro: Chapter five, lesson four. From a chain to the double helix. [[chain]]DNA is a polymer: a long chain of nucleotides. [[helix]]And two such chains wind around each other into the famous double helix. [[copy]]Today we build the chain, pair it with a second one, and watch the pair copy itself.
beats.chain: Lesson three gave us the parts of a nucleotide: a phosphate on the five prime carbon, a sugar, and a base on the one prime carbon. [[free]]Here are three nucleotides, loose. Look at the sugar of the first. On its three prime carbon sits a hydroxyl group, an O H. [[join]]The phosphate on the five prime carbon of the next nucleotide meets it, and the two join by a covalent bond called a phosphodiester bond. Water leaves, so this is dehydration, as in lesson one. [[again]]The third nucleotide joins the same way: its five prime phosphate to the free three prime hydroxyl of the one before. [[ends]]Now the chain has two different ends. One end shows a free phosphate on a five prime carbon: the five prime end. The other shows a free hydroxyl on a three prime carbon: the three prime end. [[dir]]So a strand has a direction, and we read it from five prime to three prime.
beats.backbone: Look at what the links have built. [[bb]]Sugar, phosphate, sugar, phosphate, in a repeating line. That is the sugar-phosphate backbone. [[bases]]The bases hang off it like appendages, one from each sugar. [[seq]]The backbone is the same all along, so the information is in the order of the bases. [[gene]]That sequence is unique for each gene, and one DNA molecule carries many genes.
beats.q1: Quick check. Which two positions get joined?
beats.helix: Now a second strand. [[second]]It lines up beside the first. [[anti]]But it runs the other way: where the first strand has its five prime end, the second has its three prime end. Two strands running in opposite directions are called antiparallel. [[pair]]Bases that face each other now pair up: adenine with thymine, and guanine with cytosine, always. [[hb]]Each pair is held by hydrogen bonds, the dashed cyan lines. One bond is weak, but a whole molecule has a great many. [[fit]]The pairs fit because a two-ring purine always faces a one-ring pyrimidine, so every rung of the ladder has the same width.
beats.rev: Let's read a partner strand properly. [[give]]Here is one strand, written five prime to three prime: guanine, adenine, thymine, thymine, cytosine. [[pairit]]Pair each base underneath: cytosine, thymine, adenine, adenine, guanine. [[flip]]But the partner runs the other way, so its left end is the three prime end. To read it five prime to three prime, we flip it. [[read]]It reads: guanine, adenine, adenine, thymine, cytosine.
beats.ratio: The pairing rule gives us numbers. [[a]]Suppose thirty percent of the bases in a DNA molecule are adenine. [[t]]Every adenine faces a thymine, so thymine is also thirty percent. [[gc]]That leaves forty percent, shared by guanine and cytosine. They pair with each other, so each is twenty percent. [[half]]Notice the pattern: adenine equals thymine, and guanine equals cytosine, so adenine plus guanine always makes exactly fifty percent.
beats.q3: Quick check. Use the pairing rule on the percentages.
beats.twist: Straighten the molecule and you get a ladder. [[ladder]]The two backbones are the sides, and the base pairs are the rungs. [[twist]]Now twist the ladder around an imaginary axis. [[two]]That is the double helix: two backbones spiraling on the outside, and the pairs stacked inside. [[stable]]Each hydrogen bond is weak, but thousands of them down the helix hold it together, while the covalent backbone keeps each strand intact.
beats.copy: The pairing rule also lets DNA copy itself. [[unzip]]Before a cell divides, the helix unzips, and the hydrogen bonds between the pairs come apart. [[tmpl]]Each old strand is a template. A free nucleotide whose base fits, adenine for thymine and guanine for cytosine, lines up opposite each base. [[add]]It joins the new strand by the same bond as before: its five prime phosphate to a three prime hydroxyl at the growing end. [[two]]At the end there are two double helices. Each holds one old strand and one new strand. This is called semiconservative replication.
beats.q2: Quick check. Write the partner strand.
beats.wrap: To sum up the chapter. [[w1]]Large molecules are polymers built from monomers by dehydration. [[w2]]Nucleotides, each with a phosphate, a sugar and a base, join by phosphodiester bonds into a strand with a sugar-phosphate backbone, and the order of bases is the message. [[w3]]Two antiparallel strands pair A with T and G with C by hydrogen bonds, and twist into the double helix. [[w4]]Each strand can template a new one, so DNA is copied. [[end]]Now try the chapter practice.
